paragraphs.text: Ishikawa and Tsuji (1996) described 17 patients from 12 Japanese families with familial juvenile parkinsonism suggesting autosomal recessive inheritance. Females predominated, and the mean age at onset was 27.8 years. The parkinsonian triad of tremor, rigidity, and bradykinesia was mild, but gait freezing, hyperreflexia, foot dystonia, and retropulsion were relatively prominent. All patients showed improvement of parkinsonian symptoms after sleep. Progression was slow and response to levodopa was satisfactory, but dopa-induced choreic limb dyskinesia and wearing-off phenomenon occurred frequently. The authors concluded that the similarity of clinical findings among these patients, and their differences from other types of parkinsonism, indicated that AR-JP is a distinct clinical entity.

paragraphs.text: Reports have disagreed about the role of heterozygous mutations. Poorkaj et al. (2005) concluded that although parkin disease is usually autosomal recessive, parkin heterozygosity is a risk factor for nigrostriatal dysfunction and may contribute to late-onset Parkinson disease in some carriers. (2006) found no PD in heterozygous carriers in a Brazilian genetic isolate, indicating a genuinely recessive nature, although haploinsufficiency could facilitate neuroleptic-induced parkinsonism. paragraphs.text: In a patient with early-onset parkinsonism (patient 5), Mortiboys et al. (2008) found compound heterozygosity for a 2-bp deletion in the PRKN gene (c.101_102delAG), predicted to cause a frameshift (Gln34ArgfsTer38), and a c.1289G-A transition resulting in a gly430-to-asp (G430D) substitution. The patient's fibroblasts had reduced mitochondrial membrane potential.
